name: Dentist deep cleaning (scaling and root planing)

lead: Scaling and root planing removes plaque and hardened deposits from below the gumline and smooths the root surfaces so gums can reattach more easily. It is the standard first-line treatment for periodontitis.
It is a clinical dental procedure rather than a cosmetic one, but it addresses the disease behind receding gums and tooth loss.

paras: Ultrasonic scalers and hand instruments remove bacterial deposits from root surfaces and pockets, usually under local anaesthetic, often one section of the mouth per visit.

Reported effects include post-procedure discomfort, tooth sensitivity, possible damage to cracked enamel or restorations, and aerosol generation. Results depend on home care and regular maintenance visits.

lead: Scaling and root planing, often called deep cleaning, is a non-surgical dental procedure that removes plaque and calculus from tooth surfaces above and below the gumline and smooths the exposed root surfaces. It is the usual first step in treating periodontitis, the gum disease that causes gum pockets, bone loss and eventual tooth loss.[1]

In appearance discussions it is relevant mainly because untreated periodontitis can lead to gum recession, loose teeth and tooth loss. Guidelines cited in encyclopedic sources recommend it as initial therapy, while noting the evidence base is limited because it is the standard comparison arm in trials.[1]
infobox: Dental office, usually under local anaesthetic
Maintenance visits every three to four months are typical[1]

paras: The treated area is usually numbed and typically one quadrant or half of the mouth is treated per visit. Ultrasonic scalers and hand instruments such as curettes remove deposits and smooth the roots. Optional additions include chlorhexidine rinses, locally placed antibiotics and lasers.[1] A whole-mouth approach completed in about 24 hours was proposed by a Leuven group in 1995.[1]

A 2018 Cochrane review found routine scale and polish made little to no difference for adults without severe periodontitis, but did not study root planing. A 2016 review found root planing was linked to reduced plaque and improved gingival index scores at three and six months.[1] Effectiveness is reported to decline when pockets exceed 6 mm, which may then need surgery, and home care and maintenance attendance strongly influence long-term results.[1]

Discomfort is expected afterwards, and root surfaces can be damaged, which may cause tooth or root sensitivity. Ultrasonic scaling can damage cracked enamel, early decay and resin restorations, and generates aerosols that can spread pathogens.[1]

A completed registered trial, the Kidney and Periodontal Disease Study, enrolled 51 participants with chronic kidney disease and periodontal disease.[2] Other registered studies surfaced in the search concern gum tissue classification, dental anxiety in children and crown lengthening, and do not test deep cleaning for appearance.[3][4][5][6]
